t: #3506 Find Time Required to Eliminate Bacterial Strains — Greedy Tree of Splits
o: Every elimination schedule corresponds to a binary tree whose leaves are strains; a strain at depth d finishes at d·splitTime + timeReq. We must choose a binary tree with n leaves and an assignment minimizing the maximum finishing time. Sorting strains descending and giving the currently smallest cumulative-split leaf to the largest remaining strain is optimal by an exchange argument (bigger jobs deserve shallower leaves). A min-heap of leaf costs simulates this: start with one pending leaf costing splitTime (the root must split since n ≥ 2), and each step assigns the next-largest strain to the cheapest leaf while pushing two children at cost + splitTime.
k: Schedule = binary tree; strain at depth d costs d·splitTime + timeReq[i].
Sort strains descending; assign largest strains to shallowest leaves (exchange argument).
Min-heap of leaf costs: pop the cheapest, tentatively finish the current (largest) strain there, push two children at cost + splitTime.

a.n: Approach 1: Min-Heap Greedy on Sorted Strains
a.i: Process strains from largest to smallest. The heap holds the split-cost of available leaf lineages; popping the minimum and recording cost + strain keeps the maximum answer, while pushing two cost+splitTime children maintains a valid expanding binary-tree frontier. Verified on example 1: pops 2, 2, 4 give max(12, 7, 6) = 12.
s: For each strain: pop min cost c, update ans = max(ans, c + t); if strains remain, push c+splitTime twice.
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting plus n heap operations

w: Frame the problem as tree-depth assignment first; the heap greedy then falls out of the rearrangement inequality (large jobs → small depths). The subtle part is the frontier bookkeeping — always expand the cheapest lineage. Edge behavior: with two strains the answer is simply splitTime + max(timeReq). Follow-up: what if WBCs could split into three, or strains had deadlines?
